speechtext:
The
Prime Minister stated in his speech on Tuesday that he noticed a great lack of enthusiasm on the part of the Liberal party to discuss agricultural questions when members of that party were speaking in western Canada. In fact, they seem to have left the appraisal of agricultural policy up to the farm unions and the federation of agriculture. Perhaps it is just as well. The hon. member for Essex East is not in the chamber, but I must tell him that he has not got the sympathetic ear of Canadian farmers, either in the east or the west.

I should like to deal with one item which appeared in the throne speech, and I quote:
The success ol the recent "Resources for Tomorrow" conference demonstrated the benefits of co-operation between governments in this field. My government, in consultation with the governments of the ten provinces, is examining suggestions made at that conference for co-operative measures to encourage the wise management and multiple use of Canada's natural resources.
The Prime Minister made a speech in Regina, I believe in February, 1958, in which he stated it was the intention of this party, if elected, to set up a national conference on conservation. This promise was implemented by a meeting of federal and provincial cabinet members on November 17, 1958 in order to examine ways and means of setting up such a conference.
In August of 1959 a secretariat was set up in order to determine the terms of reference. Their planning finally resulted in the conference which was held in Ottawa last October and November. I believe a summation of this conference has been distributed to the public. I do not think I anticipated these events when 1 made the following comments in August of 1958 as found at page 3506 of Hansard of that year. At that time I stated as follows:
It seems to me that a national conservation foundation, supported financially by this government and by private enterprise, could do for Canada what similar bodies are doing for other countries, and if truly national in its representation could offer logical and much needed means of bridging the gap between the efforts of federal and provincial governments and private bodies concerned in the field of wildlife management.
On examination of this summation which I have obtained of the conference held in October and November we find some tentative recommendations which have been made. For instance, on page 2 we find the following:
Many of the research problems would be substantially met by the adoption of the proposal of the research workshop-establishment of a renewable resources research council.
At page 5 of this summation we find the following:
A national, interprovincial body in the resources field, perhaps a natural resources council should be established with provision for federal and provincial finance and participation, and with a staff of its own.
At page 7 of the same document we find the following:
A national resources council should be established consisting of appointees, governmental and non-governmental, of both federal and provincial governments, whose functions would include:
(a)	Delineating resource regions and setting up, where considered desirable, ancillary regional resource councils crossing provincial boundaries if necessary;
(b)	Advising the government of Canada on national policies;
The Address-Mr. Fairfield
(c)	Suggesting to provinces programs for resource use and development;
(d)	Providing services such as libraries, information, research and engineering;
(e)	Allocating funds provided by the government of Canada to assist provinces with approved development programs.
One thing which I find is of quite a great deal of interest and which would be of great value in broadening the scope of interest in this council is to be found at page 9 of this summation where we find the following:
To be effective, this agency should be representative of the federal and provincial governments, commercial interests, universities and associations.
The studies of the conference on water and wildlife are of most particular interest, as far as I am concerned and I think to many other communities in Manitoba and throughout Canada. I am sorry to bore the house with so many quotations but I do not think this document has been very widely read and yet it is an important document. As found at page 28 of this summation I quote these two guide lines:
1.	A more positive stance in resource development matters is required in Canada. This is particularly so in "official circles" in Ottawa but is also true in the provinces.
2.	The development and management of the water resources of Canada should be based on multipurpose integrated planning which takes account of the needs for domestic and industrial water supply, recreation, irrigation, power, flood control, navigation, pollution abatement and other uses.
Again at page 29 we find the following, and I may say that this is a most significant paragraph as far as I can ascertain:
There is widespread feeling that federal participation in water resource development is based on a series of ad hoc arrangements administered by several departments without any effective coordination between them. Legislation and administration is frequently negative rather than positive -i.e., it is designed to protect the status quo rather than to search out and encourage possibilities for a more rapid development of resources.
In this respect there is a problem that affects my riding and probably affects the whole of central Manitoba as well as the city of Winnipeg somewhat. The federal government has agreed in principle with the government of Manitoba on a system or plan of flood control of the Assiniboine river valley. This has been a great problem to that part of the country for many years. Preliminary investigations on this subject were begun in 1945 and have been continued up to this time. This entails the construction of a dam at Shellmouth and a diversion at Portage la Prairie or a dam at Holland, Manitoba. It seems now that the provincial government would rather have the diversion at Portage than the dam at Holland because of the better cost benefits of the diversion at Portage la Prairie. I have lived in this

The Address-Mr. Fairfield area for some time now and there is no doubt of the necessity of control of flooding of the Assiniboine river, but, as referred to in the last paragraph which I read from the summation of the conference, I believe this is really an "ad hoc" arrangement.
Here we shall have a ditch 600 feet wide, starting at the Assiniboine river and going northward to lake Manitoba, a distance of 18 miles or 19 miles. It practically slits Canada in half. It will have seven railroad bridges and only three highway bridges across it. It is intended to carry the excess flood waters of the Assiniboine river into lake Manitoba. Those who are in authority say that this is a method of conservation of water, that they are going to store it in lake Manitoba; but as a conservation project, it seems rather odd to me, because even with fair-sized floods they admit it will raise the waters of lake Manitoba only a matter of inches. At any rate, when it reaches lake Manitoba of what use it is going to be from there on I do not know because from there most of it goes into Hudson bay and the Arctic ocean. They contemplate digging another ditch between Port-tage la Prairie and Winnipeg from lake Manitoba back to the Assiniboine in order to carry some water from lake Manitoba to assist Winnipeg in draining their sewage down the Assiniboine river into the Red river.
But what I fear about this diversion and I am afraid that many others in my area fear it as well-that it may fail as a flood control measure. At the lake end of the diversion the country is extremely flat for three or more miles and in fact it is about on a level with the surface of the lake. At times in the spring here, with strong north winds and when the lake is backing up, you will see shockingly great ice jams up against the south end of the lake, sometimes as high as 30 to 40 feet. When the water is starting to drain out this diversion into the lake and then strikes these dams of ice, in order to protect the community from flooding which would occur the dikes of the diversion, this would necessitate closure of the gates at the entrance of the diversion at the river. In other words, this would be a $12 million failure. I have asked engineers what they would do about it and they have said that they would go out and dynamite these ice jams that occur. I have never seen any ice jams broken up satisfactorily by dynamite.
When one considers the splitting in half of a whole community, in fact, practically the whole province, the cost of valuable farm lands for the project, the certainly doubtful water conservation benefits and, above all, the possibility of failure of the project as I have explained, one wonders whether the


construction of the Holland dam, though more costly, would not in the long run be of more benefit to the community and the country. It would be a true water conservation project with satisfactory flood control as well. One difference between the two, and it is quite substantial, is that the dam is more expensive. The only other difference is that instances of the Assiniboine breaking its dikes in its lower reaches and flooding the countryside would, with the dam, occur once in 80 years while with the diversion it would be once every 144 years, if the diversion works. This is my only apprehension and it certainly has not been allayed by any studies I have made of the subject.
My second interest in the report of this conference has to do with wildlife conservation and management. We all know the history of the disappearance of the carrier pigeon which occurred in our grandfathers' day and the near extinction of the buffalo which was prevented only at the last minute. As stated in this report, wildlife is a recreational resource and should be a public responsibility. Here are some of the goals as outlined in the summation on page 32:
1.	Wildlife management will continue to be primarily a public responsibility.
2.	No species should be allowed to become extinct through the instrumentality of man.
3.	Management practices will not be nationally uniform, but will vary with local conditions and the requirements of various jurisdictions.
4.	Ethical considerations are at least as important as economic considerations in wildlife management.
5.	Ideal populations of wildlife species are those that will maintain themselves without serious disturbance to their environment and satisfy the public demand for recreation. Compatibility with other interests should be sought through mutual adjustment.
6.	Adequate habitat is the quantity and quality of living space that will protect the production and distribution of ideal populations.
When one examines the figures, particularly of migratory waterfowl, one sees that the hunting pressure on this species is far more than they can stand, particularly in the United States. I think many hon. members have seen the figures and there is no point in reiterating them here. Upwards of two million duck stamps are issued per year in the United States and approximately 800,000 duck shooting licences are issued in Canada. With a population estimated at possibly 35 million ducks in North America, this means a great deal of pressure.
However, let us not forget that from the point of view of the tourist industry at least this is a tremendously important recreational resource. Here we find that despite all warnings we are depleting the capital stocks of breeding birds not only by hunting but by destroying the breeding areas by uncontrolled

drainage. Despite our history of cycles of dry and wet years, this drainage has caused a permanent reduction of breeding areas, particularly in western Canada.
All of you are perhaps familiar with the results of the drought which occurred in the thirties. At that time the duck population became very dangerously low. Fortunately, people were so broke that they could not buy licences or shells to shoot ducks so there was not the same pressure on the capital breeding stock. This is not true at this time. In western Canada we seem to be entering a dry cycle and unfortunately, or possibly fortunately, because of the economic upsurge of the country at this time under the present government people are able to afford lots of ammunition and the pressure on these birds is extremely high.
Dr. Albert Hochbaum, an internationally renowned biologist, is in charge of the Delta waterfowl research station in Manitoba and he states unequivocally that the scattered small sloughs and potholes in western Canada make up in total the most important breeding grounds for ducks probably anywhere in the world. I am happy to see that there have been consultations between Canadians and their counterparts in the United States with regard to the preservation of the integrity of the remaining areas, possibly through the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act in Canada. Perhaps this can be done on a co-operative basis between the United States and Canada and without embarrassment to the farming operations of the areas involved and perhaps even with some subsidization to the owners of the land in question.
We have got to understand that this is not only a national but an international question. We not only have to replace some of these breeding areas but we also have to change some of our hunting regulations. Many hunters will recall that in the past two years we have restricted the shooting of canvas-back and redhead ducks because their numbers are extremely low but it requires a trained biologist to distinguish these birds even at close hand. Certainly untrained hunters, and that includes most of us, cannot recognize these birds in the air. The regulations must recognize the varying habits and reproductive abilities of different species of waterfowl. In poor years this may lead to regional limitations as a protection for those places frequented by the rarer species.
Many hunters in western Canada say, "Well, if we do not shoot them someone down the line will". There is interprovincial and interstate jealousy regarding the sharing of the waterfowl supply. Publicly sponsored shooting preserves have become a blot on
The Address-Mr. Robichaud the management of waterfowl in the whole of North America. The Milwaukee Journal of October 12, 1960, had this to say about the publicly sponsored killing of Canada geese at the Horicon wildlife refuge:
Goose shooting at Horicon does not qualify as a sport. It is a slaughter. If this is what waterfowl refuges were created for, then we are no better than savages.
In this context we must gauge the need for the continuation of this species of wildlife against the recreational needs of the public, always remembering, of course, that the supply of waterfowl is not inexhaustible. In my opinion Canada has an opportunity to take the lead in shaping a modern plan of waterfowl management that is based on the life facts, and needs, of the different species of ducks and geese. In this way we may promote by example-we know, of course, at whom this is aimed-a pattern of wildfowl management that will influence practice and procedure in other regions of the annual range of waterfowl.

Mr. Speaker, in keeping with a long established custom in this house, I should like first of all to congratulate the mover of the address, the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages) and the seconder, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne). I am glad also to take this opportunity to congratulate you sincerely on your appointment to the post of Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees. We are sure you will ably fulfil your duties in this important post you will occupy during this session.
I should like also to extend my congratulations to the new Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Flynn).
I hope that, during this session, the new minister, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn), will show me the same consideration as did his predecessor.
These, Mr. Speaker, are all the bouquets I have to toss at the government, at least for the time being. I propose to find fault with the speech from the throne, as is the right and duty of any member of the opposition. However, I certainly do not propose to stoop to the level reached by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) last Saturday when addressing a group of Conservative ladies, here in this city, or when, during his speech on the address last Monday and Tuesday in this house he attacked certain persons.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, I cannot allow to go unchallenged the statement made earlier this afternoon by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) when he said that the first

The Address-Mr. Robichaud project under a joint federal-provincial program for thermal power plants was the building of the East Saint John plant. Hon. members in this house know very well that statement after statement was made last year by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Dinsdale) and the former minister of mines and' technical surveys to the effect that the federal government could not contribute to the construction of the East Saint John thermal plant, because that plant was built to use oil, not coal. Furthermore, the hon. member charged that the present government of New Brunswick was not keeping its electoral promises. The facts are that tenders were called only a few weeks ago by the New Brunswick electric power commission for the construction of the first phase of a thermal power plant to be built at Grand Lake. This plant will use coal only. This plant is designed to use 100,000 tons of coal a year in order to help the coal miners of New Brunswick. One hundred thousand tons is equal to 10 per cent to 12 per cent of the total coal production of the province of New Brunswick.
We have reached the fourth day of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. This, according to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker) own statement was supposed to be a long one. The facts are that the speech from the throne opening the fifth session of Canada's twenty fourth parliament was somewhat shorter than the one which opened the fourth session on November 17, 1960. If the Prime Minister's statement is to be accepted, I suggest we cannot help but give some serious thought to those unconfirmed reports circulated on parliament hill on opening day to the effect that the speech from the throne had been toned down by some last minute deletions.
In other words, those social and respectpaying visits to the Prime Minister's office on the opening day, first by a group of 60 members of his party and later on by a different and smaller group, could very well have been anything but social calls or respect-paying visits. No wonder that what was intended to be a long speech from the throne became a somewhat shorter speech than last year. No wonder the customary advance copies of the throne speech for the press, radio and television were suddenly withdrawn.
As this session progresses we will be in a position to judge the sincerity of the government when it implements, through new legislation or by other means, the measures described in the speech from the throne. In reviewing briefly the speech from the throne
(Mr. Robichaud.]
delivered on November 17, 1960 at the opening of the fourth session of the present parliament, I noticed certain things which I feel should be brought to the attention of this house. On page 3 of Hansard for November 17, 1960, we read the following:
Among other measures in the long range program, you will be requested to approve a number of major projects of national development. The largest of these will be the development of the water power on the Columbia river. Agreement has been reached with the government of the United States on a plan for the co-operative development of the use of these waters and a treaty will be submitted to you for approval in due course. You will also be asked to take the action necessary to fulfil Canada's part in implementing it.
When asked by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), as reported on page 16 of Hansard for January 19 of this year, whether it was the intention of the government to submit the Columbia river treaty to a committee of the house for examination during the present session, the Prime Minister replied that there was no intention of doing so. I ask now, how can we believe, how can we rely, on what we read in the speech from the throne under this government?
Again on the same page of Hansard for November 17, 1960, we find the following words:
A bill to revise the Immigration Act will be laid before you.
Those words were read by His Excellency the Governor General in the Senate chamber. There was a solemn commitment on the part of the government to undertake to revise that very important act.

On the same page of Hansard we find this:
Amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act will be placed before you to safeguard the basic purpose of the act, to strengthen the fund and to correct abuses which have developed in practice.
After the longest session in Canada's history, the government did not have the courage to face a critical situation, an unavoidable situation, which it had created by its lack of policy and its mismanagement of the nation's business. This government took office in 1957 after years of progress and

growth under the previous Liberal administration. Anyone who reads the present speech from the throne cannot help but realize there is a general election in the offing in this country and that we have here a government which is still unaware of the fact this country needs a national program, a program which can step up the rate of economic expansion and minimize unemployment in this country.
The speech from the throne, as well as the speeches delivered by the mover and seconder of the address, are nothing but self-congratulatory documents-speeches congratulating the government because in December, 1961 and January, 1962 the unemployment figures are lower than for the same period last year, a period when the unemployment record was the highest in Canadian history. There is very little in the speech from the throne which could give assurance that this government is prepared to initiate at long last a policy or a program which could result in stepping up the rate of economic growth and minimize the unemployment problem.
What is there in the speech from the throne for the Atlantic provinces? What is there for these provinces which in 1961 were relatively worse off in relation to Canada as a whole than they were in 1958 or 1960? In the first 11 months of 1961, while the rest of Canada seemed to be holding its own in average unemployment, the Atlantic provinces were showing an increase of 11.7 per cent. The slow recovery of the Atlantic region is proof that something must be done for its development; some drastic measures must be introduced to launch a regional development plan calling for large scale federal assistance to local industries, and a larger public works program by the central government.
What is being done about those very important promises embodied in the 1957 Atlantic resolutions? What about resolution No. 1, which reads as follows:
A national development program of federal assistance for developing the resources of the Atlantic provinces, having regard to their differing needs and varying financial capabilities.
What about resolution No. 2?
Industrial decentralization by placing a more equitable share of defence contract expenditures within the Atlantic provinces by the establishment of crown corporations; and by encouraging private enterprises to locate in the area and to encourage the processing here of our natural resources as a result of special fiscal consideration.
What about resolution No. 5?
Capital projects program to provide federal capital assistance for provincial projects designed to enlarge the basic economy of the area.
The Address-Mr. Robichaud
Notwithstanding the position taken by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. MacRae) in this house on January 23, Tuesday of this week, I say that those promises embodied in the Atlantic resolutions have not yet been redeemed and there is nothing in the speech from the throne which indicates that they will be honoured in the present session.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury spoke in complete contradiction of the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Fleming), who in Fredericton on October 22 last made a review of the Atlantic resolution promises and claimed that those not yet redeemed would be honoured at the next session. The hon. member for York-Sunbury gave to the federal government credit for the establishment of an electronic plant in Campbellton. The people of New Brunswick know that the plant under consideration in Campbellton, New Brunswick, is being financed by the government of the province of New Brunswick and the company's operation will be partly financed by a guaranteed loan from the province.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury has forgotten that during the Liberal administration, right in his own backyard, only 12 miles from Fredericton, the federal government spent from $60 million to $70 million for the construction of Camp Gagetown, and during those years of construction from 3,000 to 5,000 men were employed in the construction of that camp.
The hon. member, while mentioning different airports where some work has been done in recent years, seems to have forgotten Cornwallis in Nova Scotia, Greenwood and the Halifax dockyard. He seems to have forgotten the Chatham air base, St. Marguerite, the munitions depot at Renous, and again in his own constituency, the munitions depot at McGivney. He also seems to have forgotten the air base at Summerside.
There is nothing in the speech from the throne leading to the establishment of a national development fund which would result in the expansion of industrial capital in the area. Such a fund could operate jointly with provincial governments and result in the expansion of secondary industries in the Atlantic provinces. It could also take care of those capital projects which are essential and which must be undertaken if the Atlantic region is to share in the creation of lasting assets required to bring the Atlantic economy in line with that of the rest of Canada.
A situation where unemployment remains 75 per cent higher and where incomes are 40 per cent lower than the rest of Canada cannot be accepted and must not be accepted as incurable. If such countries as Britain,

The Address-Mr. Rohichaud Italy and Norway are able to cope, and to cope successfully, with similar situations, why should we in Canada allow such conditions to prevail?
On October 23 last the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) saw fit to release a statement on the Chignecto canal. This statement, ruling out construction of this long awaited project, was based on what the minister called a special study which had indicated that it would be "very unsound economics" to proceed with the project at this time.
What is still to be found out is, what kind of study has been carried out and by whom? Everyone in this house recalls the announcement made in June, 1960 by the Minister of Forestry, then premier of New Brunswick, who stated, as reported in the Chronicle-Herald for June 22, 1960:
The premier told newsmen that his government proposes to share in the payment of up to 50 per cent of the cost of a study of the feasibility of the Chignecto canal, from an engineering standpoint "in the light of modern conditions and in relation to proposed routes".
He would make the offer to the federal government, which would be asked to pay the balance of the cost of the engineering study.
On the same day, June 22, 1960, as reported at page 5242 of Hansard, the Minister of Public Works had this to say:
In reply to the hon. member for Charlotte, may I say that after consulting many times with Premier Hugh John Flemming, and the government of the province of New Brunswick, having undertaken to pay one half of the cost thereof the federal government has agreed to a survey being proceeded with to determine the feasibility of building the Chignecto canal.
Premier Robichaud of New Brunswick, as soon as he assumed power in New Brunswick after the June 27 election of that year, made it known in no uncertain terms that his government would honour the commitments made by the previous administration and that his government was prepared to pay one half of the cost of the Chignecto survey.
What results did we get? On October 21 last, the Prime Minister, in an interview in Fredericton stated in referring to the Chignecto survey that there would be a determination shortly.
As reported in the Telegraph-Journal of Monday, October 23, Mr. Diefenbaker said: "A very careful and comprehensive survey was undertaken to ascertain the economic possibilities" of the canal. He was unaware whether the survey had ended. When the study was complete the public works minister would give his views on the matter.
I repeat, the Prime Minister said he was unaware whether the survey had ended. Here was the Prime Minister, on Saturday evening in Fredericton unaware whether the survey had ended, and on Monday, October 23- 48 hours later-the Minister of Public Works 

released as a shock to the entire population of the maritimes his most disappointing and unacceptable report.
Where was the survey promised prior to the June 1960 election in New Brunswick? The people of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia have a right to know what type of survey has been carried out in order to justify the minister's statement. On what basis could a cost of $142 million be determined if the promised engineering survey had not been carried out at all?
Had the Minister of Public Works and the Prime Minister already forgotten a report which was tabled in the House of Commons on January 19, 1953, part of which reads as follows:
The commission finds that at the present the economic returns to the Canadian people on the investment in the proposed South Saskatchewan river project are not commensurate with the cost.
This, however, did not prevent the present government from signing an agreement with the province of Saskatchewan for construction of this project on July 25, 1958.
How can we believe a Prime Minister who states on October 21, at a press interview, that he was unaware that a survey had ended, when as we have every reason to believe, only a few days before, the whole matter had been discussed by the cabinet and the Minister of Public Works had been instructed to prepare a statement on the whole matter?
How can be believe the same Prime Minister when a few weeks later in Charlottetown he tried to impress his audience by declaring that the long proposed causeway to link Prince Edward Island with the mainland was economically feasible? How could he know so little about the Chignecto canal and pretend to know so much about the causeway when, according to the Minister of Public Works' own admission in this house on January 22, no official or preliminary reports had been made available to the Prime Minister prior to his visit to Charlottetown on December 6 last?
The citizens of the maritime provinces have reacted to the bombshell dropped on them by the Minister of Public Works on October 23 last. The government cannot ignore the demand of the maritimes population and the Chignecto canal must become a reality.
The Prime Minister must be reminded again and again that no public project anywhere in Canada can do as much for an area as the Chignecto project can do for the Atlantic provinces. This offhand dismissal of the whole idea is not being accepted hands down by the citizens of the maritimes, and the present government has no right to base

its appraisal on such an incomplete assessment of all factors, whether engineering or economical.
As I stated earlier, while the Canadian economy demonstrated some growth during 1961, it was not the stable and continuous growth which Canada enjoyed from 1950 to 1957. While during these years the gross national product increased at an average rate of 5.6 per cent annually, the facts are that since this government took office the average increase has been less than 1J per cent annually.
What has been the performance of the Atlantic provinces in this supposedly booming year of 1961? According to statements which we hear every day in this house coming from the government side, we must accept it as a satisfactory situation. I have here a report produced by the Atlantic provinces economic council dated January, 1962, and this report gives a summary of the performance of the Atlantic region. Population increased by 1.8 per cent. Well, the federal government cannot take credit for that, I am sure. The labour force went up by 4.4 per cent. Here again, no credit can be taken by the government. It is true that employment itself increased by 3.6 per cent, but, at the same time, unemployment went up by 11.7 per cent during the period. Is that a satisfactory situation?

The speech we have just heard ended on a note presently being sounded by many prominent members of the opposition about an alleged decline in Canada's prestige throughout the world. Statements like that cannot be allowed to go without question, and I intend to deal with the matter. Just a few minutes ago we heard the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam talking about his experience at the United Nations. It seems that everybody who goes to the United Nations becomes an expert on that great world organization. The hon. member told us about conversations he had down there with people who expressed dislike for Canada's policy and for Canada itself. Apparently he agreed with those statements.

He himself was quite prepared to downgrade Canada, and to proclaim in the House of Commons that in his opinion, and that of some of his dubious friends at the United Nations, Canada's prestige is not as high as it used to be. His party is right behind him in his efforts. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is struggling to achieve disarmament. We all know the history of the world during the last 30 or 40 years and the great difficulty there has been in maintaining peace, difficulty negotiating with communist countries, and difficulty pertaining to attempts to achieve disarmament. Yet, in the face of all the disappointments he has had throughout his lifetime, he is carrying a torch in this great endeavour to maintain peace in the world and to effect disarmament.
What man could pursue a greater cause in the face of the disappointment of earlier years? In spite of that the Leader of the Opposition, who served in the capacity of secretary of state for external affairs, at-temps to discredit the present occupant of that office and, to my great regret, both inside and outside the house lends the weight of his experience and authority to suggest that Canada's influence in world affairs had decreased, the inference being that when he was secretary of state for external affairs Canada's international status was never greater.
I well remember the late Gordon Graydon, the former member for Peel, being our spokesman on external affairs, and the close co-operation that existed between the opposition and the government in the field of international affairs. The late Mr. Graydon supported the then secretary of state for external affairs, realizing the difficulties of his position and realizing that, for the benefit of Canada's stature in the world, the Canadian parliament should present a united front. That situation prevailed until the Suez crisis in
The Address-Mr. Churchill 1956 when the then secretary of state for external affairs was not at his best. I will not recite the situation that prevailed in those days. I offered criticism, as did others of the action of our then secretary of state for external affairs. However, we did not downgrade Canada. We did not say that Canada's international reputation was destroyed because of the mistakes he made during that crisis. We pointed out those mistakes but we did not downgrade our own country.
Similarly, Mr. Speaker, Canada's stature in international affairs has never been higher than it is under the leadership of the greatest prime minister of our day, namely, the present Prime Minister. Who, among the leaders of the world, had the courage at the United Nations a year ago to stand up and lay before the United Nations and the world the situation with regard to Russia and the falseness of the Russian position in pretending that it is not an imperialist power and that it is not subjugating nations which have come within its sphere of influence? It was our Prime Minister who did that and he received world acclaim for so doing. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that Canada's stature in world affairs has not been diminished one iota, since this government took office.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext:
They are not good representatives of Canada abroad. I know that you yourself, Mr. Speaker, have travelled very widely. I suggest that if you go to any country in the world, outside of the iron curtain countries, you will find that the name of Canada is held in the greatest esteem and for very good reasons. There is no obligation undertaken by Canada under the United Nations that she has not fulfilled. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite this: Have you already forgotten the

The Address-Mr. Churchill war in Korea when Canadian soldiers, airmen and representatives of the navy played their full part? Have you already forgotten our troops who are in the Gaza strip between Israel and Egypt and who have been there in rotation for years performing their duty in behalf of maintaining peace? Have you already forgotten our men who are in constant danger in the Congo? Have you forgotten our men who have been standing guard in Europe for so many years?
Canada has been playing her part in all international affairs where assistance has been required of a military nature and has similarly played her part where assistance has been required on the economic plane. Canada has never failed to pay her share of the cost of the United Nations, has never failed to respond to requests for food for the underdeveloped countries, has never declined to assist the various other operations conducted by United Nations bodies, whether it is with regard to medical care, health education or providing educational opportunities.
There is no field in which Canada has not been playing her part internationally. We are one of the leading members of NATO, an organization which is set up and maintained in order to preserve our freedom. I may mention the Colombo plan. My hon. friends opposite can share with us in any credit that is due Canada under the Colombo plan and I may say that a great deal of credit is due. We co-operated with them in days gone by when they proposed appropriations for the Colombo plan and they have co-operated with us similarly. Under the Colombo plan Canada has played her full part with other nations of the world in assisting underdeveloped countries.
Just a year ago I had the good fortune to be in India at the official opening of the Canada-India atomic reactor in Bombay. Full praise was given to Canada's assistance in that operation by Prime Minister Nehru, by representatives of his government and by the people who were assembled there on that occasion. I had the good fortune to go into the state of Madras where, under the Colombo plan, Canadians and Indian engineers and the people of India have constructed great hydroelectric works. The reception afforded our party is almost beyond description.
We travelled through some 15 to 20 Indian villages in the state of Madras, and at every village there was an arch expressing welcome to the Canadian representatives. At every village the villagers turned out to shout again and again, "Canada", "Canada". Thousands of people in that area know Canada and

know what Canada has done. Ten thousand of them worked on the dams and on the works in that Kundah project. The word "Canada" is there on large boards. It is inscribed permanently on bronze plaques in buildings that have been erected at the power stations. The people of the province of Madras who worked on the dam and those who are benefiting from the electric power supply know the word "Canada", are happy to meet Canadians and speak highly of Canada.
The same is true in Pakistan. One of the finest hydroelectric developments in southern Asia is at Warsak. The great dam was built there by Canadian engineers and skilled Canadian technicians, with the assistance of the people of Pakistan themselves. It is a great monument to Canada's efforts to assist an underdeveloped nation. The people of Pakistan, from President Ayub Khan down, could not fully express their appreciation of all that Canada has done. You cannot tell me that Canada's name is not held high in India and Pakistan. There is no discrediting of Canada in those two countries.
The same is true in Europe. Not a country in western Europe has anything but good to say with regard to Canada. Canada is known in western Europe. There is the friendliest feeling for Canada in western Europe. You have only to go to France, Belgium or Holland, as I have done as the representative of the government on trade matters or with regard to the Canadian wheat board or as the representative of the government to attend memorial services at Vimy Ridge or at the cemeteries in Belgium and Holland, to find out that this is so. Irrespective of the particular field of endeavour that one represents, I have found nothing but respect and praise for Canada and an understanding of Canada which the people of these countries find it difficult to express.
You cannot tell me that Canada's name is not held in high regard in these countries. France, Belgium and Holland have not forgotten the contribution Canada has made in two wars. These things remain in the hearts of these people and, although there may be the odd criticism here and there of some action, basically the people of these countries have nothing but the highest regard for Canada and the Canadian people. On some other occasion I hope to inform the House of Commons of the great respect, care and attention which the people of these three countries that I have mentioned pay to the sacrifices made by Canadians in both world wars.

I put it to my friends here in the House of Commons that these reports about Canada's name being held in low regard at the United Nations have no resemblance to the truth whatsoever. Two or three disgruntled representatives of some country at the United Nations find fault with Canada over something that may have happened but that does not represent the feeling of the people of these various countries. All you have to do is to visit the countries to see what the reaction of the people is. Canada's name is held in high regard.
Canada is respected for several reasons. As I have said, Canada has played its full part with respect to its obligations under the United Nations and has been playing its full part in NATO all these years. Canada is recognized as a country that has no selfish ambitions for power and as one which makes no demands upon other nations. Canada is recognized as a generous country that is ready to help, ready to exchange students, ready to exchange technicians, ready to send doctors, nurses, scientists and engineers abroad to assist in countries which are developing.
Where in all of that is disrespect for Canada? Where in all of that has Canada lost her prestige throughout the world? She has not lost it at all. It is higher than it has ever been and those people in this country who pose as experts on the United Nations, as experts with regard to the opinion of people in other countries, are not fooling anyone at all. They do not know what the situation is in other countries of the world. Let them stand up here and tell us what country of the world is finding fault with Canada other than some iron curtain country. I challenge them to put the names of these countries before us. Oh, no, they do not want to embarrass those dubious friends of theirs at the United Nations. They do not want to get themselves involved in some way with some peculiar type somewhere in the world. Oh, no. They will not disclose that information. They will decry Canada. Canada is this, that and the other thing. Canada's reputation, they tell us, has been destroyed.
Not one word of that is true. Canada's reputation is high and Canada's prestige throughout the world will be retained under the leadership of the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Foreign observers see in this country a stability of government which they did not recognize in 1956. They see a stability of government which they recognize as good for this country and good for the world.
The Address-Mr. Churchill
Within the British commonwealth of nations Canada's position is still the same and still assured. There is the greatest friendliness within that organization. Our party has always stood for a strong commonwealth of nations. Not so with the Liberal party across the way. I pointed out in 1956 that I had gone to the trouble of reading all the speeches that had been made by the Leader of the Opposition when he was secretary of state for external affairs. I kept notes of all his speeches to see on what occasions he had mentioned the commonwealth. He almost never mentioned the commonwealth or did so simply by way of an aside if there was to be a commonwealth conference. I examined all his speeches in the House of Commons and he never mentioned the commonwealth unless in response to a question. That represents the stand of the Liberal party with regard to the commonwealth. On the other hand, our party has always been strongly in favour of a strong commonwealth. We have supported the commonwealth and will continue to do so.
I hope there will be an end in this debate or subsequently to these disparaging remarks about Canada's prestige in world affairs, these disparaging remarks with regard to one of the greatest members of the House of Commons, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, these disparaging remarks with regard to the leadership afforded by the Prime Minister. This is not the way in which Canada should present herself to the world. We can have all sorts of differences locally-and there are plenty of things on which to differ-but as far as world opinion and international affairs are concerned we should show a united front. That is not being done at the present time in the light of what was said by the Leader of the Opposition just the other day. This is not good for Canada and no one knows better than the Leader of the Opposition the damage that can be done to Canada's reputation abroad by statements such as he made in the house the other day.
I suggest that if the name of Canada, a country which has given so much in the past and which is continuing to make such a great contribution at the present time, is to be maintained as it has been down through the years responsible Canadians must not downgrade our country. For a small country Canada has made proportionately as great a sacrifice during the last 40 years as any country in the world and Canada is prepared to continue in all the efforts that are now being made to defend ourselves in case of necessity, to negotiate in order to preserve the peace and to lend all our efforts for the preservation of peace. Let us not forget our young men scattered throughout the world at the present time

The Address-Mr. A. Brassard and our young men in Canada who are standing on guard hour after hour in case of necessity. Canada is playing her full part and Canada's name should be praised and not downgraded in the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join those who spoke before me in congratulating the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages) and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) for the honour the government has bestowed upon them by asking them to be respectively the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I also wish to commend the Deputy Speaker, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau). I wish him success in his new office. We hope, or rather we are sure, that he will perform his duties with understanding, judgment and impartiality, the more so since he will have you as an example, Mr. Speaker.
The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) also deserves congratulations for having been appointed Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. I wish him and the new parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard), every success.
Like most hon. members, I have followed closely the speech which was delivered by the leader of the Liberal party (Mr. Pearson) during the debate on the speech from the throne, and I wish to say that seldom have 1 been as proud to be a Liberal and to have for a leader the hon. member who spoke in this house on Monday. I know that those feelings are fully shared by my colleagues.
His comments reflected common sense and moderation. In spite of what the hon. members opposite may think, he has drawn a true picture of the state of affairs in Canada, and that is why his speech hurt. It did indeed, and the pain it caused may be seen in the fact that there were 74 interruptions by seven ministers, not to mention those by private members.
Do you know who won the competition? None other than that man of a few words, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). No, it was not the Prime Minister. I would say that it was on the part of the minister, a bit of a revenge for the 1956 convention. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) was well ahead with 46 interruptions.
Would you like a few samples from his stock of words, which paint him better than the best painter's brush could? Here are a few:


Nonsense . . . That is not true ... Silly talk .. . Lies . . . Foolish statement. .. Misrepresentation ...
And there are many others. All on fields in which, it must be agreed, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has long shown himself to be an expert.
The runner-up was the Right Hon. Prime Minister with seven interruptions. He surely deserves a certificate of merit. His interruptions, although not so numerous, were a little more insidious.
I am sure it will not please my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) nor the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill) to hear me quote some statements and some views set forth by the Prime Minister, and then say what I think of such behaviour in this house.
On page 39 of Hansard for January 22, 1962, concerning a copy of the speech from the throne sent to the Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister stated:
The hon. member received a confidential copy in the usual way. Did he respect the confidentiality of that document, or did he make it available to others?
Mr. Speaker, whoever has carefully studied the two men since 1957 cannot but wonder that such a question should have been put by the one who has asked it. He should be the last one to doubt somebody else's statements, especially those made by the leader of the Liberal party, who is known as a man who has always shown the highest regard for truth and the oath of office.
And what are we to think of that other inference, of a truly personal nature, made by the Prime Minister, and which I find on page 73 of Hansard:
I want to tell the hon. gentleman this: that is one subject, softness on communism, that he should not discuss.
The Prime Minister was indeed justified in stating during that same speech:
To increase one's own prestige in one's eyes it is not necessary to run down another.
He was really speaking "ex cathedra" when he talked that way.
The third one was the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) with his six interruptions. I must admit that they were slightly less numerous than those he made during the famous pipe line debate.
Fourth in line, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) with four.
Ex-aequo in fifth place, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker).
Now, sixth in line, we see the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) to whom we shall give a consolation prize.

No doubt, the speech of the Leader of the Opposition helped further aggravate the almost open sores of the present administration.
When I speak in this way, it is not because I am despaired, as I am not here to get myself re-elected, no more than are my fellow members.
We are here to look after the public's interests and, from time to time, pass judgment on those of our colleagues who, in our modest opinion, may show weaknesses in carrying out their responsibilities.
I not only listened to the Prime Minister but also admired the elegance and flourish of his gesture which invariably precedes his word in the best tradition of ancient Roman rhetors. I also admired the varied modulations which expressed a great variety of feelings, and I also admired the great ease with which he passed from the angriest to the most amiable tones.
Mr. Speaker, may I point out that it is six o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, before the house recessed I was saying how much I had admired the performance of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) last Tuesday, during the debate on the address in reply.
Neither should I fail to mention his great facility for resorting to irony and sarcasm and more particularly the incredible agility of his gyrations among his colleagues, an agitation which gives us an almost unique and priceless opportunity to study him in profile, from the back, in full face, half and three-quarter face, from half back, semi-profile, in short in all the postures very peculiar to him and which command the required applause.
I also discovered in him a rather doubtful talent for imitation. Perhaps, because of one of his more recent statements he has, this year, dropped one of his favorite practices which consisted in looking straight and insistently at the press gallery. If he ever decided to make peace with the newspapermen and return to his old love, I should hardly be surprised if he became one day
The Address-Mr. A. Brassard the half pleased recipient of an "Oscar" which, for him, would admirably replace the Nobel prize for peace.
His final scene in the last parliament, in 1958, had left me dumbfounded. However, I realized that having been some time in opposition he could not be expected to forsake his true nature so soon. The display and the show we witnessed Tuesday morning appalled me. Just to think that the performer was the first citizen of my country. If he ever deigned to glance at my humble remarks, he would doubtless have a taste of the medicine so often served to others, and if he realized what others feel under such attacks, he might perhaps decide to leave to others in his party who are well qualified in this field and able to do that kind of work such a task unbecoming to the Prime Minister of my country.
Conservative members complain when we speak like this. Some of them-not all of them fortunately-speak one way and act differently.
If we challenge what they do or what they say, we are accused of working against national unity. Mr. Speaker, this way of thinking reminds me of the strong protests of somebody who would try to strangle you and be shocked if you shouted for help.
Mr. Speaker, shortly before the six o'clock recess, the hon. member for Bumaby-Coqui-tlam (Mr. Regier) charged the Liberal party with using mean and fraudulent tactics in the election held in two neighbouring ridings of Toronto. He contended that the Liberal party was responsible for the distribution of certain communist pamphlets. He also asserted in a most assured way that the electoral machinery of the Liberal party in Toronto had been used to make phone calls, ostensibly from representatives of the communist party, to advise voters to cast their ballots for the candidates of the new party.
The hon. member stated moreover that this campaign could not have been the work of the communists, on the ground that they did not have the required means. Now-I am only addressing myself to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam-I must say I am rather surprised to find him so well informed on the financial status of the communist party, for it is usually a well kept secret.
I might add, again for the benefit of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, that I would not be surprised if the communist party really conducted this base attack. We have a party called the social credit rally which has a 15-minute television program every week during 26 weeks a year, and to my knowledge, that party has no official source of income.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex West):

speechtext:
I appreciate very much the privilege of participating in this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne which was very ably moved and seconded by the hon. members for Laval (Mr. Bourdages) and Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne). In doing so I wish to go on record as supporting the address and most emphatically opposing the amendments to it.
I have listened with interest to the remarks of the last speaker, the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard), and cannot help but feel he was a bit unfair-indeed it might be put more strongly than that-in accusing the government of using old age security allowances, old age assistance, blindness and disability allowances in such a way as to favour one section of the country as against another. In fact I do not see how he can contribute to unity and good fellowship in all parts of the country by accusing the government of that kind of conduct.
The contents of the speech from the throne indicate that the government will continue

to serve the best interests of all sections of the country, fairly and impartially. Recent articles in the press divulged that the government has fulfilled some 50 or 52 of 60 promises it made, and the measures outlined in the speech from the throne will certainly contribute very substantially to the fulfilment of election promises made in the 1957 and 1958 campaigns. The promise made to our elder citizens that their interests would not be forgotten will be fulfilled by the proposed increase of $10 per month in old age security. Recipients of old age assistance and the blind and disabled will be provided with similar increases by co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. The needs of the farmers will be met by acreage payments in the prairie regions and in other parts of Canada through price supports and stabilization of prices under the Agricultural Stabilization Act.
Of exceptional importance, I believe, is the information contained in the throne speech that conferences are being held with the various provinces concerning the amendment of our Canadian constitution and that agreement has been reached on methods for accomplishing this objective in our own Canadian parliament. Ratification by the provincial governments of this agreement will mark the completion of Canadian sovereignty.
Of paramount importance also is the intention of Canada to begin the construction of an electric power grid from coast to coast. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Dinsdale) told the northern development conference in Edmonton last fall that whereas only 22 per cent of Eskimo children had access to school in 1957, 60 per cent of these children are now in school, some of them already in high school, and that by 1968 there will be a place in a classroom for every child of school age in the Northwest Territories. The territories themselves are also being reorganized and will have two districts instead of one. The two councils should be able to give closer attention to the needs of these areas.
These developments clearly show that the present government has in no way lost the vision which the people of Canada found so appealing in 1957 and 1958 and which I would predict they will again find appealing in 1962.
We have some national problems which are grave, and there are plenty of these problems. Time does not permit us to cover much of this ground in the time allowed to each member who speaks. However, there is one of these problems to which I should like to draw some attention and on which I should like to make some comment. It concerns our butter surplus.
The Address-Mr. Thomas
I should like to commend the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) for the efforts he put forth in order to bring before the members of this house and the country generally the situation as he sees it. He put a great deal of effort into the preparation of his speech. I cannot agree with the solution he suggested. However, he put on the record a great deal of information.
One of the promises which helped to elect this government was that the farmers of Canada should have a greater share of the national income. With this objective in view the government three years ago increased the support price of butter from 58 cents to 64 cents per pound. Because our housewives are buying 25 cent margarine instead of 64 cent butter, we have accumulated upwards of 200 million pounds of butter which is surplus to our requirements. Because butter tends to deteriorate if kept too long in storage, the surplus has proven to be an embarrassment to all concerned. There is no market for this surplus outside of Canada. Butter is available on the world market at half the price of our product. We therefore cannot dispose of it outside of our own country without being accused of dumping. It is doubtful that the domestic market can be expanded to an appreciable extent as margarine has been found to be a generally accepted substitute and it is available at less than half the price of butter.
I do not suppose that any agricultural problem has been given as much consideration during the last two years as has the matter of this butter surplus. I wish to commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) and the government for one thing in particular, namely for not reducing the support price on butter. I submit that we cannot assist the farmers to obtain a greater share of the national income, as was promised, by cutting the prices of their products; nor do I believe that cutting the price of butter would contribute any appreciable relief to the present situation. The farmer's expenses are inclined to be rigid; and if the price of his product is cut, his only alternative is to produce more units in order to satisfy his requirements. The solution lies rather in diverting our small surplus production of milk to other uses, preferably for use as a supplement in the rations of hogs, poultry and veal calves. This diversion should take place before the milk leaves the farm and before the costs of transportation, processing and other possible costs are added to it.
The Dairy Council of Canada, at their recent convention, requested the government to solve this problem by subsidizing the consumer price of butter to the extent of 14

The Address-Mr. Thomas cents per pound while maintaining the support price at its present level of 64 cents per pound. The weakness that I see in this proposal is that we have no reasonable assurance that the remedy would be successful. It was found by Great Britain and the Netherlands some years ago, when they were faced with a similar problem of the substitution of margarine for butter by housewives, that the buying habits of the consumer were not changed until the price of butter was dropped almost to the level of the price of margarine. I think this situation could be explained by the fact that those people who find margarine an acceptable substitute at a cost of 25 cents per pound are not likely to return to their butter-buying habits until butter can be purchased for approximately the same price. It would likely be found that the purchasers of margarine are those who are most influenced by economic considerations and they are not likely to purchase butter unless the prices are nearly comparable. The proposed subsidy of 14 cents per pound would therefore probably not result in diminishing our butter surplus.
Again, I think another weakness in this proposal is that the domestic market is still consuming 75 per cent of all the butter produced in Canada. Therefore only 25 per cent of our production is surplus. If a general subsidy of 14 cents per pound were applied, we would be subsidizing unnecessarily three pounds out of every four pounds. We would therefore be paying for four pounds or 56 cents per pound for every pound of surplus that we disposed of. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is too expensive a way to solve the problem.
I would suggest that the solution lies in the more complete organization of the dairy industry under marketing boards through which the producers themselves can take the necessary steps to prevent the very small surplus of milk production from exerting undue pressure on the price structure of the dairy industry. Milk is the most universal agricultural product in Canada. Production of many farm products is confined to limited areas but milk is produced almost everywhere. When the dairy industry is depressed the whole of our economy suffers.
No matter how we undertake to support the dairy industry, the surplus will find its way to the point of support. We tried skim milk powder and got into trouble with the surplus. We changed from skim milk powder to butter and we are now in trouble with that. There is no solution to this problem, I submit, except to control the surplus at its source and have the milk fed to farm animals before it gets into the channels of trade.


Press reports indicate that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec are at present reviewing their milk marketing legislation with a view to more effective organization of the dairy industry in these provinces and if these areas, where about 70 per cent of the milk in Canada is produced, are brought under closer control then a small surplus should not be permitted to depress dairy prices, and if the milk can be fed to livestock on the farm the build-up in our dairy butter surplus should be stopped. Nothing effective can be done until the build-up in our butter surplus is stopped. If this can be done, I think it will not be too difficult then to find ways and means of disposing of the surplus. We can dispose of it as we disposed of our canned pork. Coupons could be given to those whose incomes are small or who are in receipt of welfare payments of various kinds so that they could buy butter at a price level the same as that of margarine. There are other ways that it could be done but I can see no point in speculating about ways and means of getting rid of our surplus until we have managed to find some means of stopping the build-up of that surplus.
I should like to place on the record several comments concerning the dairy problem made by leaders in the industry at the dairy farmers of Canada convention held in Montreal last week. Mr. Frank E. Lutes, president of the dairy farmers of Canada, is reported in the Western Producer of January 25, 1962, as having stated that there is an urgent need for a national milk plan. He is quoted as follows:
Lest there be those who fear the element of compulsion suggestive in board marketing, let us consider that the lack of direction and planning in our national production is posing some real compulsion at the moment-compulsion to reduced income on the part of a great number of dairymen.
Mr. Romeo Martin, general manager of the Quebec co-operative federee, said that a steady increase in butter production since 1949 has been coupled with a steady decline in domestic consumption and that more margarine and other substitutes were being consumed each year and many Canadians were cutting down on fats in their diets. He said that better equilibrium between production and consumption is essential but should not be sought by lowering production since present farm cash income is much too low.
Again we come back to the point I have tried to make that farm requirements are quite rigid and that if you cut the price of the farmer's product his only recourse is to increase the number of units produced which only adds to the problem. Mr. Martin is reported as having said that Canada's butter surplus had no outlet in foreign trade and

that world prices were much below Canadian prices. The convention recommended that quotas be established on fluid milk production, based on each producer's production in 1961.
It is quite evident from the news reports of that convention last week that the dairy-farmers themselves are quite aware of the need for some measure of production management and with both producers and governments working on the problem it will likely only be a matter of time until a solution will be found which will prevent the accumulation of unmanageable surpluses of butter. Then the butter surplus can be reduced without unduly disturbing the price structure of the industry.
I wish to refer to one or two other matters before I conclude. The various programs of the federal government for the promotion of better living conditions in all parts of Canada have proved to be beneficial to my constituency of Middlesex West. Our appreciation goes out to the government for the new post office building now under construction in the village of Delaware. Plans are being prepared also for new public buildings at the village of Lucan and the town of Strathroy. The government is participating with the province of Ontario in the construction of the $1 million Parkhill dam. Seventy five per cent of the cost of a new $1 million extension to the Strathroy district collegiate institute to serve as a composite high school will be contributed by the federal government. The province will contribute the other 25 per cent. A grant of $243,000 was made toward the construction cost of the new Strathroy hospital.
Numerous extensions to rural mail routes have been allowed to provide better service to individuals who have been able to qualify under the revised regulations. House to house service in the suburban areas of the city of London has been widely extended as suburban development has proceeded. The Hutton side-road overpass has been completed and the grade crossing fund under the control of the federal government stands ready to contribute 50 per cent of the cost of the new four-lane overpass on Oxford street west as soon as the city has completed its plans for the rebuilding of that traffic artery.
I feel that this opportunity should not pass without mention of the fact that the Queen's guineas prize for baby beef steers has been won by junior farmers in Middlesex county for the past three years in succession. This award was instituted many years ago and was called the King's guineas, and it has now become a special prize of $250 awarded to the boy or girl who feeds and exhibits the best 26207-1-15J
The Address-Mr. Badanai baby beef animal from the province of Ontario at the royal winter fair at Toronto. This year the winner was Shirley Earley of R.R. No. 3, Kerwood; the 1960 winner was John Giles of Glencoe and the 1959 winner was another of the Earley clan, a cousin of the 1961 winner. This is an indication of the very fine type of livestock that is produced in Middlesex county. Full credit must be given also to the young people concerned for their skill in feeding, training and exhibiting these animals.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I feel very strongly that this government has done a wonderful job of administering the affairs of this country. I feel that they continue to offer the best hope for continuing government of the people, by the people and for the people of Canada.
