speechtext:
It is
a great privilege, Mr. Speaker, to speak on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I shall use the limited time at my disposal to make a few observations and suggestions which, without being presumptuous, I submit with sincerity.
First of all, sir, I should like to congratulate you upon your appointment as Deputy Speaker. I have had occasion to observe your fine qualities and friendly attitude which will ensure success in the discharge of your duties. I should like also to congratulate the new Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Flynn). If he achieves the success in his new position that he achieved as deputy speaker during the past session, then I am sure he will enjoy a successful term of office. Congratulations are also in order for the mover (Mr. Bourdages) and seconder (Mr. Browne, Vancouver-Kingsway) of the address who, in their speeches-leaving the usual exaggerations aside-displayed remarkable enthusiasm for what the throne speech contained. Under the circumstances, this is quite understandable.

The Address-Mr. Badanai
It is true that the speech contains some measures which are good and will receive unanimous support, such as the legislation designed to increase old age pensions, pensions for the blind and disabled. We were happy to learn that steps will be taken to set up a contributory old age pension system, conditional upon the agreement of the provinces. I am informed, however, that this procedure is not really necessary. The government has the power to introduce a contributory system of old age pensions without an amendment to the British North America Act. The appointment of an independent commission to recommend the redistribution of federal constituencies is to be commended, provided the members of this commission are selected after consultation with, and approval of, the leaders of the opposition parties. The increase in federal loans to finance exports and the broadening of the Small Businesses Loans Act are measures that may well prove beneficial and will receive my support, as will the increase in assistance for the education of the children of the war dead.
The rest of the speech, however, with the exception of a few localized handouts, contained vague and guarded references of a miscellaneous nature but nothing tangible was said about a national program which would expand our economy and create employment on a mass scale. The unemployment picture may be a little better than it was, but not much. I have just received a report from a northwestern Ontario commission on unemployment. This is a body of men appointed by the mayors of the two lakehead cities, Fort William and Port Arthur, to study the problem and offer suggestions. Questionnaires were mailed to more than 3,000 employers and 120 union locals. Replies were received from 800 employers and 27,000 men and women. These have disclosed that since 1956 the rate of growth of jobs at the lakehead has slowed down to one third of the rate in the early 1950's.
Between 1951 and 1961 the twin city population increased by over 25,000 persons. The population has increased by 35 per cent and the job opportunities have increased by only 12 per cent. The immediate result has been an increase in unemployment, particularly since 1956. There are about three times as many unemployed registered now as there were in 1951. The population increase will have its major effect on employment between 1963 and 1970. By 1966, there will be at least 1,200 extra job seekers coming from the schools each year. Our present rate of increase in jobs is about half the required rate. It is therefore obvious that the government must make strenuous efforts to meet the employment problems in the years ahead.


While I have been pointing out the difficulties in the district of Thunder bay, everyone knows that this is also the experience of other regions in Canada.
The establishment of a capital development fund to encourage secondary industries and employment-creating development, administered by an advisory council, should be considered at the earliest possible moment; and the establishment of a municipal road fund to enable municipalities to expand their services and construct much needed municipal projects.
The ultimate goal of the government should be a real attempt to enact employment policies which would provide the substance of the right of the individual to be gainfully employed. The country is tired of hearing the recital of accomplishments of the government, many of which in reality are without substance. There is recovery, but there are no jobs.
No doubt many hon. members have had the experience of talking with a jobless man, married and with a family. You get the feeling that he has to fight a constant battle against frustration. Unemployment insurance benefits may keep his body together, but what will keep his spirits up? All around him are the signs of a prosperous community and he is not a part of it; and those who are part of it, in some instances treat him as a second-class citizen. Unemployment is by far the biggest problem facing the government today.
The kind of economic policies and measures contemplated in the speech from the throne will not provide enough jobs in the time immediately ahead. It is a serious and complex problem which requires a concentrated effort in relation to which, up to the present, the government has given no dynamic leadership.
The speech from the throne did mention the need to bolster the unemployment insurance fund. The special committee appointed by the government to study the question of the unemployment insurance fund-which has taken a severe beating in the past four years- will in its own good time recommend some action which I hope will place the fund on a sound actuarial basis.
The latest figures of the dominion bureau of statistics seem to show that seasonal unemployment is something apart from chronic unemployment. It is an occurrence even in good times of full or near full employment and should be dealt with separately.
During a debate on a supply motion last September I suggested that consideration be given to setting up two separate systems with separate funds, one for seasonal workers and the other for non-seasonal workers. The latter would serve non-seasonal workers, which was

the purpose for which the unemployment insurance fund was originally established-to give regular workers some degree of protection against loss of wages during brief periods of unemployment. Such a fund should be as nearly self-sustaining as possible, while the other fund would require substantial annual assistance from the government. Since a decision has to be made soon and the day of decision cannot be postponed indefinitely, I sincerely trust that this suggestion will be considered by the government.
On various occasions I brought to the attention of the government the need for a new building to house the unemployment insurance commission in Fort William, which now occupies an old, dilapidated building which served as a post office 30 years ago when the city had less than half the population it has today. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) is well aware of the situation and agreed with me that a new building is the only solution to this problem.
Recently it has been suggested that the present post office, which cannot be operated efficiently any longer-it lacks space to take care of the present postal traffic, which has increased threefold, and the location does not lend itself to an extension of facilities or an extension of the building-should be relocated and a new post office should be built on the site where we hoped the new unemployment office would be constructed, moving the present unemployment insurance commission office to the present post office building. This move would be history repeating itself 30 years after a similar move had been made. This is not my suggestion; it has been suggested to me by those in authority in our city. However, I do suggest that the departments concerned give serious consideration to these matters as soon as possible.
Another project that would help the employment situation in the lakehead area and which could be undertaken as a winter works project, is the extension of the existing administration building at the lakehead airport and the extension of airfield runways to handle Vanguards and other large aircraft.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) announced in Fort William last April that $650,000 had been appropriated by the Department of Public Works for this project. Only a few days ago I was advised that treasury board, in their review of the Department of Transport estimates, had reduced to $100,000 the amount for this project to commence late in the fall. This is a disappointment, as we anticipated that the work on the airport would mean employment for several hundred men early in the year.
The speech from the throne differed very little from the generalities of other throne
The Address-Mr. Badanai speeches to which I have had the privilege of listening. One passage which struck me as being rather obscure was the reference to the promotion of world trade. It did not propose any line of action. It simply said something to the effect that the government has renewed promises of support for the expansion of world trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis. What does it all mean?
What a contrast to President Kennedy's recent state of the union message in which the president spelled out the movement of the United States toward lower tariffs and freer trade. Had the speech from the throne contained a proposal that the government would examine the possibility of joining the European common market, and given assurance of definite action for early implementation leading up to the immediate creation of a north Atlantic market with the gradual removal of tariff barriers on either side of the Atlantic, such a statement would have been something to cheer. But instead there was a sidestepping of the issue with meaningless phraseology.

speechtext:
After I am through, I will. Japan has adopted a program of trade liberalization affecting many products which we export, notably, pulp and paper packing, wrapping and tissue paper, nickel and forest products and many other items. This liberalization of trade has been made possible by the high international evaluation of Japan's ability for expansive economic growth. Where does our Canadian prospect for economic growth stand? The prospect for economic expansion is closely related to the tariff and tax policies of the government which, so far, have been deficient in the real promotion of trade, and no amount of genial salesmanship on the part of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) can be regarded as an effective substitute.
There is not a word in the speech from the throne about trade with Latin America, though this is a field which, if properly cultivated, might yield an appreciable harvest. It has been reported that Dr. Raul Prebisch, executive secretary of the United Nations economic commission for Latin America, expressed the thought that the people of Latin America would welcome the opportunity of sitting round the conference table with Canadians to explore whether there are any fields in which mutual trade can be expanded. South America's 150 million people could offer a new and substantial market for Canadian products. In 1960- I have not the figures for 1961-we purchased approximately $270 million worth of

The Address-Mr. Badanai goods from South America, while they only purchased from us something like $127 million worth.
The continent of South America appears to be ready to accept a new concept in international relations and trade, in the hope of exchanging their products for manufactured goods and machinery which at their present stage of low technological development they cannot hope to produce themselves.
The field is, therefore, wide open for Canada to sell her manufactured goods in this rich market. Such goods are badly needed in Latin America to help the economic balance of those countries and, in exchange, we would receive valuable natural products. Let us not forget South America when we are considering the expansion of our exports.
Another disappointing feature in the speech from the throne was the total absence of any reference to tax cuts. I know that some will say: how can taxes be cut at a time when welfare costs are to be increased? The way to cut taxes is simple: just cut them. We can learn from the experience of other nations, an experience which has shown that lower taxes often mean higher revenues. This is because more goods can be sold at lower prices. One has only to look at the phenomenal success of food markets and chain stores for proof of this contention. They have shown that low prices and high volume run up larger profits.
The truth of the matter is that far from having recovered its buoyancy, as we have been led to believe by this government, the Canadian economy is still going backwards, and the fact remains that in the absence of meaningful tax reductions there can be little prospect of a lasting improvement in our economy.
Last October I visited Italy. I was particularly impressed by the tremendous economic progress which a country so poor in natural resources has achieved during the past few years. Italy's gross national product for 1961 was expected to have reached, by the end of the year, the highest percentage increase ever recorded. Industrial production, also, was expected to reach an increase of 15 per cent as compared with the previous year.
I asked officials of the government and leading men in industry whom I had the privilege of meeting what was the secret of this prosperity. The reply I received was to the effect that the recovery of the Italian economy, which had been in the doldrums after the war, was no miracle but, rather, the result of common sense in applying efficient methods of manufacturing and

production and flexible government tariffs and export policies, including a moderate tax incentive policy, to aid exports. We would do well to ponder the reasons underlying the success in world markets achieved by a country as poor in natural resources as Italy.
I also visited Israel. Here, indeed, is something to behold. In spite of very limited natural resources and a small population the per capita productivity of this country is simply amazing. They have a productivity council, one of the most successful of its kind, and with the aid of the government it is training 4,000 students a year in industrial management courses. It is to be hoped that when the Canadian productivity council gets into top gear-and I am afraid it is running in low gear now-it will make Canadians more conscious of the need for productivity than it has been able to do so far.
The Montreal Gazette of January 24 has an editorial on this subject from which I wish to quote a paragraph:
The competition that Canada faces in her trade with the world is along a vertical, as well as along a horizontal line. That is to say, she must compete not only with the industries of other nations as they are today; she must be preparing to compete with these industries as they will be in a few years time, say by 1970. To win today (difficult as that is) will not be enough, if Canada will lose tomorrow.
It was generally anticipated that the speech from the throne would disclose information that an amendment to the Immigration Act would be introduced at this, presumably, the last session before the general election. However, the Prime Minister decided on an order in council approving a formula which changes the regulations. This course was taken as a substitute for a change in the act. The statement read by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) last Friday with reference to regulations which will make it possible for immigrants in all parts of the world to enter Canada if they can qualify in respect of education, training and other skills is supposed to be an improvement on the former regulations. This seems to me to be just another way of saying to a prospective immigrant, if for any reason he or she is not wanted: we are sorry, but unfortunately you do not meet the requirements of our regulations so your application for admission to Canada is therefore not approved.
My friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) aptly described the new regulations when he said:
The hon. lady has said that the new section 31. which is substituted for section 20 of the existing regulations, abolishes discrimination. Of course, it does nothing of the kind. It substitutes one

The Address-Mr. Ricard
set of criteria for discrimination for another. I am one of those who think that the words "discrimination" and "selection", as any dictionary shows, mean precisely the same thing, and they cannot mean anything different. The hon. lady is well aware, as she has said previously in the house, that there is in the existing regulations no racial or other similar discrimination, and I am glad there is not going to be any such discrimination now.
But I suggest that what the hon. lady has done is to make it necessary to look at every individual case and compare it with every other case, and that, by abolishing some of the convenient general categories she is going to create an administrative problem that it will be absolutely impossible to cope with if we are to have any substantial immigration. Of course, if the pattern of 1961 is to be followed, when we had a net emigration from this country, it is probable that the new regulations are well designed to serve that end.
Finally I should like to point out that what the government undertook to do five years ago was, not to change the regulations but to change the act, and that has not been done.
Feet that once trod pavements in Britain and Europe are now wearing two and one third million pairs of Australian made shoes and sandals, and this means an extra factory-bench in shoe factories to every ten existing previously. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I am going to reserve my criticism of the minister's statement until we can see how the new regulations are going to operate. The provision for the admission of a wider list of non-white immigrants who have relatives in Canada, and the broadening of the type of appeals which may be taken before the immigration appeal board, is a welcome change with which few, if any, can quarrel. However, the unfortunate fact is that in 1961 fewer people immigrated to Canada than emigrated from the country, mostly emigrating to the United States.
No one is advocating wide open doors to all and sundry, but I cannot let this occasion go by without expressing concern at the slow flow of desirable immigrants which, for all intents and purposes, has been practically stopped since 1960. Those of us who retain faith in the growth and development of this great and glorious country which we are proud to call our own, believe that desirable immigrants should advance our economic and cultural well being, and be capable of creating a Canadian industrial development by enlarging Canada's domestic market.
What is the worth of an immigrant? The department of immigration of Australia has the answer to this question which in effect, means that before an immigrant begins earning and spending, each adult immigrant worker's value, as he walks to his bench or desk, or to the construction site of a building, has been calculated by Australia's federal treasurer, at $15,000. This is the official cost of feeding, rearing and training an Australian born child up to the working age. Today, every tenth shop girl in Australia's shops owes her place behind the counter to the growing demand which immigrants are creating and helping to fill.

Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes that remain, I should also like to comment on the unconsidered statements which have been made in this house in the last few days. Opposition speakers have tried to make us believe that Canada's prestige with the other commonwealth nations was declining.
Mr. Speaker, as you were in our group, you know that I had the advantage of going around the world two years ago, and that I attended the commonwealth parliamentary conference in Canberra.
At that conference, I was able to meet parliamentarians from all the commonwealth countries and I discovered with pride that Canada was held in very high esteem and was very much respected by people, as well as its Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green).
I also had the opportunity, last October, to attend the NATO conference in Paris. There again, I had contacts with parliamentarians from every country and, to my great satisfaction, I found among them an unparalleled esteem and respect for Canada. When hearing some remarks like those made in this house by people who are supposed to have great experience in the matter, for instance the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), I may well say that, apart from being surprised, I was deeply affected.
Far from throwing discredit on our country, far from belittling the prestige it enjoys and should enjoy abroad, I feel that we should use all possible means to boost Canada, because it is a great country, which commands universal admiration.
Wherever we went-and you are aware of that as well as I am, Mr. Speaker, since you were a member of the party-when we uttered the word Canada, when we said we

Division
were Canadians, we were greeted with open arms and with these words: "I would like to live in your beautiful country".
This is quite different from what the members of the opposition would have us believe and it is quite different from the disparaging comments these gentlemen put on record.
